passage:
Coach's note, Neelam, exam mentoring.
Neelam failed the final round of her civil-service exam for the third time in March. In our session that week, I began to say, "This may open other doors," and stopped, because I saw her face. She said, "Please don't tell me it's a blessing." I said I wouldn't, and we just sat.
For two months she didn't mention the exam. In June she came and said, "I keep thinking about how scared the first-timers are at the centre. I know how it feels." She asked if she could help run the Saturday nerves-and-planning session for new students.
I did not suggest the meaning. She found it in her own time. I gave her the room and the schedule, and I'll be checking in with her monthly.
— Seema, coach

qa.q: How many times had Neelam failed the final round of the exam?
qa.a: Neelam had failed the final round three times.

qa.q: What did Neelam feel when the coach began to say that this may open other doors?
qa.a: Neelam was hurt and did not want to hear a silver lining. Her face and her request not to be told it is a blessing show the pain was still fresh.

qa.q: What did Seema do that helped Neelam build her own meaning?
qa.a: Seema stopped offering a lesson, sat with Neelam, gave her time and later offered a room and schedule when Neelam asked to help new students.

qa.q: How did Seema see the difference between saying the pain had a purpose and Neelam finding one herself?
qa.a: Seema seems to see that meaning offered too early feels false, while meaning Neelam found in her own time could last. That is why Seema did not suggest it.

grounding: After a failure, a person slowly builds meaning in her own time; the coach avoids forced silver linings.

passage:
Tuesday, 11:20 pm.
The shop closes on Friday. I signed the last paper today and put the key in an envelope. Gautam came by with samosas and said, "Everything happens for a reason." I nearly threw the tea at him. He meant well. He looked so awkward that I let it go, but I wrote "no" on my palm with a pen afterwards.
It's not that I think there's no lesson. It's that I don't want it yet. It still feels like a hole in the floor.
Tonight, though, I opened the notebook and wrote three things I'd never do again with suppliers. It didn't fix anything. It just sat there on the page, small and true. Maybe that's how it starts. Not tonight though.
— Disha

qa.a: The shop was closing on Friday.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when Gautam said everything happens for a reason?
qa.a: Disha was angry and hurt, nearly throwing the tea, though Disha saw that Gautam meant well and looked awkward.

qa.q: What small step did Disha take that night that was her own?
qa.a: Disha wrote three things never to do again with suppliers. It was a small, true note in Disha's own words, not a consolation someone handed her.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt after saying everything happens for a reason?
qa.a: Gautam probably felt awkward and unsure how to help. He came with samosas because he cared, and his face showed he did not know what else to say.

grounding: After a failure, a person slowly builds meaning in their own time; a forced silver lining feels false but a small lesson of their own does not.
